unit.can_do_en: ask about a form and say what I need.

brief.situation_en: Maria calls the bank. Tiina answers.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Hi! My bank card has gone missing.

judge.reason: Same greeting and same statement: my bank card disappeared; only register differences (moi/hei, mun/minun, katos/katosi).

lines.speaker: Tiina
lines.text_puhe: Voi ei. Mä suljen sen heti. Mikä sun nimi on?
lines.text_kirja: Voi ei. Minä suljen sen heti. Mikä sinun nimesi on?
lines.gloss_en: Oh no. I'll block it right away. What's your name?

judge.reason: Same: I'll close it right away, what is your name; only pronoun register differences.

lines.speaker: Tiina
lines.gloss_en: OK, the card is now blocked.

judge.reason: Okei/selvä are register variants; the card is now closed in both.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Good. Can I get a new card?

judge.reason: Both ask whether I can get a new card; saanks mä = saanko minä.

lines.speaker: Tiina
lines.text_puhe: Joo. Se tulee postis viikon päästä.
lines.text_kirja: Kyllä. Se tulee postissa viikon päästä.
lines.gloss_en: Yes. It comes in the post in a week.

judge.reason: Joo/kyllä are equivalent; it arrives by post in a week in both; postis = postissa.
Both ask whether it costs anything; maksaaks = maksaako.

lines.speaker: Tiina
lines.gloss_en: No, a new card is free.

judge.reason: Both say no, the new card is free; uus/uusi and ilmanen/ilmainen are spoken variants.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Adds -ni for 'my': pankkikortti becomes pankkikorttini. Speech just says mun pankkikortti.
Kadota 'to go missing' adds -si for the past: katosi. Speech drops the last i: katos.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. Speech says it the same way.
Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.
Adds -n for 'I': sulkea becomes suljen, the k turning to j.
Se with -n when the whole thing is the object: kirjoittaa sen.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
'What.' A question word in nominative singular, asking what the price is.
Sinä with -n for 'your': sinun. Speech shortens it to sun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for your
forms.why_en: Adds -si for 'your'; nimi turns its i to e first: nimesi. Speech just says sun nimi.
Means 'is': present tense, 3rd person singular, going with 'Helsinki'.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Means 'now'. Leo asks where home is at this time.
From sulkea, to close. Suljettu means 'has been closed'. The k changes to j.
Means 'good!' or 'great!', showing you are happy.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 1st person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.lemma_meaning_en: to get, to be allowed to
forms.why_en: Saada adds -n for 'I' and -ko to ask: saanko. Speech says saanks.
The genitive singular matches kortin: uusi becomes uuden, the si turning to de.
As the thing you get, kortti takes -n: kortin, tt turning to t.
Yes. In everyday speech people often say joo instead.
'It.' Nominative singular, referring back to the price.
Tulla, to come, in the form for he, she or it: tulee.
Adds -ssa for 'in': posti becomes postissa. Speech drops the last a: postis.
The genitive singular goes before päästä 'after': viikko becomes viikon.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: maksaa, to cost, with the question ending -ko: maksaako? Speech uses -ks: maksaaks.
The partitive singular of jokin 'something': jotain. People say it the same way.
Means 'new', describing Maria herself: 'I am new here'. Spoken: 'uus'.
Speech drops the i in the middle: ilmainen becomes ilmanen. Books write ilmainen.
